About

I'm a final-year Product Design Engineering student at Loughborough University, finishing in December 2026.

The short version is that I'm a maker. I've spent three years learning to model in SolidWorks, Siemens NX, Fusion 360 and AutoCAD — and just as long learning to machine, mill, solder, print and cut the results out of metal and plastic. The part I enjoy most is the handover between the two, where a design meets the tolerances of the real world and usually has to change.

Most of the work below was done in teams, which is how engineering actually happens. I've noted what was mine on each one.

Outside the workshop I play violin, piano and saxophone, cook a lot, and take photographs. My final year project came directly out of the violin playing.

Final year project · 2025–26

Automated Acoustic Testing Rig for Bowed String Evaluation

A machine that bows a violin at a constant speed, so strings can be tested without a human holding the bow.

Violin acoustics are normally tested with an impulse hammer — strike the string, measure the response. It's fast and repeatable, and it characterises the body and bridge well. What it cannot do is reproduce what happens when somebody actually plays.

Bowing is a continuous stick-slip friction cycle, Helmholtz motion: the string is dragged until its restoring force overcomes static friction, slips back, and catches again. That sustained cycle feeds energy in continuously and excites torsional vibrations a single hammer strike cannot physically trigger. To compare how a steel-core string performs against a synthetic one, you have to bow it.

The difficulty is that bow velocity sits in a narrow envelope. Too slow and static friction dominates, giving a scratchy, aperiodic tone; too fast and the hair fails to grip, giving a thin surface sound. The rig was designed around a steady 10–30 cm/s, because acoustic amplitude scales with bow speed and any motor cogging or stuttering would appear as artefacts in the data.

To build it on a student budget I bought a hobby RC car and repurposed it. One purchase supplied a drivetrain, suspension struts, brushed DC motors and an electronic speed controller for a fraction of the cost of sourcing them separately. I then measured every relevant part with digital calipers, rebuilt them as parametric CAD, and used those models as fixed reference geometry so the custom brackets, carriage adapters and sensor housings would fit without interference — all designed for 3D printing.

The first prototype's failures shaped everything after it. I suspended the violin on bungee cord to avoid damping its resonance; under bowing load it oscillated and the sound profile was unusable, so the design moved to a rigid aluminium extrusion matrix. The RC receiver then refused to initialise below roughly 70% power — a voltage threshold lock I couldn't design around — so I bypassed the antenna and receiver entirely and routed power through the onboard switch, letting an external voltage controller govern speed without tripping it.

The maths was the check on all of it: a 12 W power budget, and a 6 V supply against a 40 V rating — a 0.15 ratio that put a number on why the first build stalled under load — then gear ratio, output torque and rosin friction to show the drivetrain could hold the carriage at speed.

I also specified the validation the rig needs before it can be trusted: tracking carriage velocity with a rotary encoder or optical tracking to quantify fluctuation, mapping normal force with a load cell to confirm the bow neither dips nor lifts across its stroke, and running an accelerometer on the frame with the bow disengaged to check the motors don't sympathetically excite the violin body.

Status: design and virtual validation complete, with the first prototype built and tested. Physical fabrication of the final design is the next stage, followed by calibration and comparative testing of steel-core against synthetic-core strings.

Manufacturing & workshop practice

Single-Cylinder Air Engine

Machined from raw stock by a team who mostly hadn't used the machines before. It ran at 1,130 rpm.

Every part — cylinder, base plate, manifold, backplate — was turned or milled from bar stock by hand. Only one of the five of us had meaningful workshop experience beforehand, so the rest learned the machines as the project ran. That made us slower and, we decided, more careful.

We split into turning and milling sub-teams, each person owning their own parts and checking someone else's. Finished parts went into a common drawer so anyone could test fit against them.

It worked. The engine reached 1,130 rpm at 20 psi, and nearly every part came in inside the 0.25 mm tolerance — most under 0.1 mm. Where other groups had to spin their engines by hand to start them, ours turned the moment air hit the manifold.

It wasn't clean. The manifold was machined out of tolerance and had to be remade near the deadline, costing us the time we'd wanted for a full pre-submission check. Our conclusion was that final inspection should have been a scheduled task with a name against it — not something we assumed would happen.

One controller, five CAD packages

Joy-Con Reverse-Engineering CAD Study

Five of us modelled the same Nintendo Joy-Con, each in a different package, then compared what each was good at.

Take one object with awkward, genuinely difficult surfacing — a Switch Joy-Con — and have five people model it from scratch in five different tools: Fusion 360, Siemens NX, SolidWorks, Onshape and Blender.

I built the Fusion 360 model and render. Modelling something designed to sit in a hand is unforgiving — the surfaces are all slight compound curves and nothing is truly flat, so any shortcut in the sketch geometry shows up immediately in the render.

What came out of it was a practical sense of where each package earns its keep — parametric solid history for engineering intent, mesh and material tools for presentation — and enough exposure to five interfaces that an unfamiliar one doesn't throw me.

Mechatronics · Python on LEGO SPIKE

PID Line-Following Robot & Colour Sorter

Two robots, a printed track, and a control loop tuned until the wobble went away.

A buggy that follows a line using a reflected-light sensor and a PID controller written in Python, which then hands its cargo to a second robot that tips it into a colour sorter.

The proportional term is the easy part — sensor reads off-target, wheels turn at different speeds to correct. The other two make it smooth. The integral term accumulates past error so the robot corrects a persistent drift instead of fighting the same offset forever. The derivative term watches the rate of change and starts correcting before the robot has wandered, which is what kills the oscillation.

Balancing those three constants is entirely empirical. You change one, watch it wobble, change it back.

Our write-up listed what we'd do next: a wider wheelbase for stability, a stronger rear wheel so we could drop the rollers, and code to make the tipper wait for the second robot rather than assume it had arrived.

Engineering Management & Modelling

Catapult: Mathematical Model & Physical Modifications

Predict where it lands, modify the machine so it lands there, then compete.

Six weeks, a supplied catapult and a target. Two deliverables: an Excel model that would output the correct firing angle for any target distance and projectile mass, and physical modifications to make the thing repeatable.

The model was built from first principles — spring constant, unextended spring length, beam inertia, plasticine density, catapult geometry. Spring length changes continuously through the throw, so the cosine rule is applied at every degree of rotation to find extension, and exit velocity converted to initial angular velocity. We tested real springs on a tensile tester to calibrate the constants rather than trusting the datasheet.

On the hardware side we 3D-printed a sight, a rear hook and stabilisers in three heights so the geometry could be swapped and re-tested.

The competition returned 12 points from 9 shots — less than the model promised. The gap between predicted and actual is the genuinely interesting part of this project.

Siemens NX + CAM · Reverse engineering

CNC Manufacture, DFM & Design for Assembly

Two parts taken from CAD model to CNC-cut metal, then measured to see how much the process lied to us.

The core of this was writing and optimising CAM programmes in NX to cut two parts, then measuring what came off the machine against what we'd modelled. That meant full process plans — tool by tool, with cutting speeds and feed rates for every operation from facing through profile milling, hole milling, spot drilling and reaming.

We researched limits and fits and used them to produce PMI documentation, so tolerance intent travelled with the model instead of living in someone's head.

My part was the Part B modifications and the design changes for ease of assembly — moving features so they could actually be reached, and adding tactile and visual guidance so parts could only go together the right way.

The interesting failure was in quality control: with limited measuring equipment, some complex geometry simply couldn't be verified. Knowing you can't measure something is its own finding, and it changed how we'd scope the next one.

Coordinate Metrology

Measured a supplied two-part assembly against drawing specification and issued pass / re-measure / re-machine / scrap decisions on each feature, plus a recommendation on whether to accept the batch and continue the supplier contract.

Reverse Engineering & 3D Printing

Reverse-engineered bicycle components — training wheel assembly and mudguard — from measurement through CAD to printed part, sliced and produced on Bambu Lab machines.

Battleship — Python GUI Game

A playable multiplayer Battleship in Python and Tkinter: settings panel with input validation, scoring with a time bonus, leaderboard, sound feedback and 1–4 player turn rotation. Built to explicit interface principles — consistency, feedback, error prevention and visual hierarchy.

SpaceX Facility Tender

Costed a hypothetical manufacturing facility end to end: transport modelling across the UK and US, materials supply and storage, scrap recycling, inflation and exchange-rate exposure, VAT and corporation tax — delivered as a tender model and planning gateway.

Materials & Manufacturing Analysis

Analysed material selection and manufacturing routes for four products — a maraging-steel golf club face, a vulcanised rubber Vans outsole, a cold-impact-extruded aluminium fire extinguisher body, and a graphene tennis racquet head.
